subject: Sophisticated Ways of Losing Interest: Uncertainty and Time

messages.author: 7d2a96af532ed7de
messages.subject: Sophisticated Ways of Losing Interest: Uncertainty and Time
parts:
Dear List,

Once again, thanks for Stan!

I'm stumped with a modelling problem that feels like it would be a common one, and seems related to Gaussian processes, state space models, Kalman filters, and the other clever stuff I see people talk about on here (and which unfortunately, is a bit beyond my understanding at the moment).

I thought I'd chance posting it, in case a type of model was immediately obvious to any of the resident experts!

I suppose I have two questions:
  • Can anyone think of a sensible model for the problem?
  • Can anyone imagine how to implement my weird verbal description of a model in Stan?

Say I have N people, in J groups, who all have opinions which change over time. I have R Likert survey responses from them, say 0-20 per person, which have come in at random points in time (over say 10 years). I guess we could consider them observations of a latent opinion variable. At any given time, most individuals have 0 responses.

I'm interested in predicting the individual opinions of the N people at the present time - e.g. if they were forced to respond to a survey right now. Overall, changes in responses over time are Gaussian about 0, where the SD of that distribution increases as a function of their response(s) getting older.

Ideally, for individuals who had never responded, the prediction would be a partially pooled group parameter. For individuals that had responded, as those responses get older, the individual's estimate would creep towards the group J prior, and eventually just become it (e.g. responses have got so old that they are irrelevant).



I've hacked together a few very simple models for this, based around estimating a single real[0,1] parameter, which, multiplied by T, serves to weight an average between the group prior and the response. So when T == now, the response gets all the weight. The problem is, for those who have responded a lot, more prior mass gets thrown into their person-level estimate (an average of the weighted averages from each response), and person-estimates become less certain for serial responders, where we might expect the opposite to happen (for people with low response variance, at least).

The only other thing I can think of is an ARCH type model on individual response variance (score difference ~ time difference), used to add uncertainty as a function of time to each response, and then for each individual, multiply all their time-fattened response probability-distributions (one for each of their responses), along with the group prior, to arrive at a person-level posterior. However, I have no idea how I'd code this in Stan, and it seems a bit harebrained considering that this sounds like a problem that may have been solved before!

Does anyone have any ideas? (And if you read this far, bless you!)

> Say I have N people, in J groups, who all have opinions which change over time. I have R Likert survey responses from
> them, say 0-20 per person, which have come in at random points in time (over say 10 years). I guess we could consider
> them observations of a latent opinion variable. At any given time, most individuals have 0 responses.

With response of 0--20, it might make most sense to just treat
it as a constrained continuous value, rather than, say, as an ordinal value.

You can get predictions alpha in (-inf,inf) back to (0,20) with:

20 * inv_logit(alpha)

> I'm interested in predicting the individual opinions of the N people at the present time - e.g. if they were forced to
> respond to a survey right now. Overall, changes in responses over time are Gaussian about 0, where the SD of that
> distribution increases as a function of their response(s) getting older.

Then you can treat the alpha as varying by individual and over time in
the way you suggest.

Yes, you could use Gaussian processes for this, but it might just be
simpler to code it up as a simpler time-series model.

> Ideally, for individuals who had never responded, the prediction would be a partially pooled group parameter. For
> individuals that had responded, as those responses get older, the individual's estimate would creep towards the group J
> prior, and eventually just become it (e.g. responses have got so old that they are irrelevant).

So the value's multilevel, with a group response at a time, perhaps,
then an individual's response at a time. Both of these could be time
series.

beta[t] = intercept of group over time

beta[t+1] ~ normal(beta[t],sigma_beta);

alpha[i,t] is individual i at time t

alpha[i,t+1] ~ normal(alpha[i,t], sigma_alpha);

predicted_response[i,t] <- 20 * inv_logit(beta[t] + alpha[i,t]);

response[i,t] ~ normal(predicted_response[i,t], sigma_response);

Or something like that. It may take some index juggling if
you don't have full data of every respondent at every time.

It lets you predict going forward by having alpha[i,t] and
beta[t] for which there is no data.

> I've hacked together a few very simple models for this, based around estimating a single real[0,1] parameter, which,
> multiplied by T, serves to weight an average between the group prior and the response. So when T == now, the response
> gets all the weight. The problem is, for those who have responded a lot, more prior mass gets thrown into their

> person-level estimate (an average of the weighted averages from each response), and person-estimates become /less
> /certain for serial responders, where we might expect the opposite to happen (for people with low response variance, at

> least).
>
> The only other thing I can think of is an ARCH type model on individual response variance (score difference ~ time
> difference), used to add uncertainty as a function of time to each response, and then for each individual, multiply all
> their time-fattened response probability-distributions (one for each of their responses), along with the group prior, to
> arrive at a person-level posterior. However, I have no idea how I'd code this in Stan, and it seems a bit harebrained
> considering that this sounds like a problem that may have been solved before!

I think it'll be easier just to use a multilevel time series
in the usual way, where a parameter varies over time, with each
time increment adding noise to the previous time estimate.

Having said all this, I don't have a lot of experience in this
area and someone else probably has a better, more standard way to
do this.

- Bob
